challenges.situation: Your company needs to pick a date for a cross-team offsite. There's no scheduling tool and emails aren't getting responses. You notice everyone keeps referencing 'the first Monday after quarter-end.' What's happening?

options.text: A focal point is forming — 'first Monday after quarter-end' is culturally prominent enough that everyone expects everyone else to converge on it
options.feedback: This is a Schelling focal point — a solution that emerges because it's 'obvious' given shared context (quarterly rhythm is shared knowledge). It doesn't need to be optimal or decided by authority. It just needs to be the answer everyone expects everyone else to pick. Social proof plays a minor role, but the focal point preceded any explicit mentions.

options.text: Someone with authority already decided and communicated it informally
options.feedback: Not quite. This is a Schelling focal point — a solution that emerges because it's 'obvious' given shared context (quarterly rhythm is shared knowledge). It doesn't need to be optimal or decided by authority.

options.text: It's the objectively optimal date because workloads are lighter after quarter-end
options.feedback: Not quite. This is a Schelling focal point — a solution that emerges because it's 'obvious' given shared context (quarterly rhythm is shared knowledge). It doesn't need to be optimal or decided by authority.

options.text: Social proof — once a few people mentioned it, others just followed
options.feedback: Not quite. This is a Schelling focal point — a solution that emerges because it's 'obvious' given shared context (quarterly rhythm is shared knowledge). It doesn't need to be optimal or decided by authority.

challenges.situation: Bitcoin has over 100 million users coordinating around the same rules despite never meeting or trusting each other. Many technically superior alternatives exist.
challenges.question: What force keeps coordination locked on Bitcoin?

options.text: Uncertainty — switching to an alternative is risky because you can't be sure others will switch too, so everyone stays at the existing focal point
options.feedback: The core force is coordination uncertainty — even if an alternative is better, you can't use it unless everyone else moves too. Focal points are self-reinforcing because the cost of unilateral switching is total loss of coordination. This is uncertainty about others' behavior, not trust in Bitcoin itself. Scarcity and identity are effects, not the coordinating mechanism.

options.text: Trust — people trust Bitcoin's track record more than newer alternatives
options.feedback: Not quite. The core force is coordination uncertainty — even if an alternative is better, you can't use it unless everyone else moves too. Focal points are self-reinforcing because the cost of unilateral switching is total loss of coordination.

options.text: Scarcity — the 21 million cap creates value that alternatives can't replicate
options.feedback: Not quite. The core force is coordination uncertainty — even if an alternative is better, you can't use it unless everyone else moves too. Focal points are self-reinforcing because the cost of unilateral switching is total loss of coordination.

options.text: Identity — Bitcoin holders identify with the community and resist alternatives
options.feedback: Not quite. The core force is coordination uncertainty — even if an alternative is better, you can't use it unless everyone else moves too. Focal points are self-reinforcing because the cost of unilateral switching is total loss of coordination.

challenges.back: The solution that emerges when people must coordinate without communicating — not the best option, but the most obvious one given shared context

pairs.right: Attempting to displace an existing focal point — requires creating new prominence, not just better features

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Optimizing for quality
scenarioA.text: My proposal is objectively the best option. If I explain why it's superior, everyone will rationally converge on it. The best idea wins.

scenarioB.label: Optimizing for obviousness
scenarioB.text: The best idea doesn't win coordination games — the most obvious one does. I'll make my proposal maximally prominent, simple, and easy-to-expect. I need others to predict that others will predict my option.

challenges.explanation: The second response shows structural awareness — recognizing the game and changing it, rather than just playing harder within the existing frame.

principle.text: Coordination without communication is solved by focal points — options that stand out to everyone because of shared cultural context, prominence, simplicity, or precedent.

reflection: What's the focal point in your team or industry that everyone follows without questioning? Did someone design it, or did it emerge by accident?
